title: Photography direction for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: Photography for a B2B SaaS company site
excerpt: Photographs should show the product doing a job. A feature grid and a stock office scene do not argue. Each frame needs a claim you can say in a sentence.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. The article is about choosing pictures that show a product, not a pile of undifferentiated icons.
caption: A screen full of equal icons is the picture to refuse when one job should lead. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should photographs on a B2B SaaS site show?
faqs.answer: Show the product doing a job, cropped so the relevant record and action are readable. The sentence beside the picture should match the pixels. A lobby, a handshake, or a closed laptop does not carry that claim.

faqs.question: When is stock photography a poor fit?
faqs.answer: Stock is a poor hero when the claim is about your product, because the product was not in the room. A real screen, even a simple one, is stronger. Wait to add people until you can photograph the actual work.

faqs.question: How should alt text be written for these pictures?
faqs.answer: Describe what is in the frame, in a sentence a person who cannot see it can use. Name the record and the action when they are visible. Do not paste a slogan or a keyword list into the alt text.

markdown:
B2B SaaS company website photography should show the product in use. The picture is part of the argument, not a mood pasted under the headline. An operator who already runs software will trust a readable screen of the job long before they trust a lobby, a handshake, or a laptop shot from across a room.

Reject a feature grid with no job, and reject the photographs that exist to decorate it. If a picture does not help someone see the work, it is occupying the space where the work should be. Choose fewer frames. Make each one a claim you can say in a sentence.

## A picture is a claim

Every photograph on this site argues something. A real queue with a status argues that the job has a place to live. A blurred office argues that you rent an office. The operator is buying the first. They will assume the second or ignore it.

Write the claim before you choose the frame. "An admin sees which approvals are waiting and who owns them." Then art-direct toward that sentence. If the frame cannot carry the sentence, it is the wrong frame. Crop, reshoot, or use a product capture instead of a scene.

Put the claim in the layout as a nearby sentence, not as a hope that the picture will be self-explanatory. Interfaces need a line of context. People need a line when the people are the subject. The line should match what is actually in the frame. A caption that invents a story the pixels do not show is the same failure as a feature tile that invents a job.

One claim per picture. A hero that tries to show the product, the team, the city, and the feeling of confidence shows none of them at a size anyone can read. Pick the product. Let the team have a quieter frame on the about page, where the claim is about who does the work.

## Show the product in use

Capture a screen at a size where the job is legible. The status, the primary action, the record people came to judge. Simplify the data. Use realistic structure. Blur secrets. Do not redesign the product into a smoother fiction for the sake of the photograph. This buyer compares pixels to tools they already know. Fiction loses.

Show a person only when the person clarifies the job. Hands on a known screen. An admin at the step the headline names. The face is optional. The task is not. A portrait with no task belongs beside a name and a role, not in the hero where the product was promised.

Prefer a still you control over a metaphor. Ladders, mountains, compasses, and open roads are borrowed drama. The operator has a queue, not a summit. If you need atmosphere, let it be the light on a real desk where the screen is still the subject. The room can be calm. The room should not replace the interface.

Use a sequence when one frame cannot hold the decision. Before the approval and after it. Two frames, each with a claim. A sequence is still an argument. A collage of six features is the grid again.

Hanabi's public product work, including Got Next and Leadly, is built around a job and a small set of actions. That is the standard to borrow for photography, even when the photographs are of someone else's product. Show the action. Leave the rest out of the frame.

## What to reject

Reject the feature grid as a picture. Six icons in a row, each with an abstract noun, photographed as if they were a scene, still have no job. An illustration of the grid is the same object. Cut it and spend the space on one screen.

Reject stock of strangers pointing at charts you cannot read. Reject the overhead of a notebook, a plant, and a closed laptop. Those frames are pleasant and they make no claim about the software. Pleasant is available everywhere. The claim is not.

Reject a dashboard where every chart is the same size. It photographs as importance without hierarchy, which is the opposite of a job. If the real product has that problem, the photograph has found a product issue. Fix the screen or choose a different screen. Do not shoot the confusion and call it comprehensive.

Reject images you do not have rights to use, and reject customer screens you do not have permission to show. A blurred illicit capture is still a breach of trust. Build a demo record and photograph that. The structure can be true while the names are fictional. Say so if a careful reader might think it is a live customer.

## Direction you can hand to someone with a camera

Write a one-page brief. The job in a sentence. The screen that proves it. What must be readable. What must be excluded. The rooms and faces you do not want. The aspect the page needs, including a vertical crop for the phone.

Include the words that will sit next to the picture, so the photographer is not guessing at a mood. If the sentence is about an overdue approval, the frame should feel like attention, not like a party. You do not need to art-direct feelings with adjectives. Direct the objects.

Ask for the screen at full clarity and for a wider frame that shows the desk only if the desk helps. You can crop later. You cannot invent sharpness that was never captured. For interface work, a direct product capture in the browser is often better than a camera angled at a monitor. Glare and moiré ruin the claim. A clean capture, set in a simple scene if you need a scene, keeps the pixels honest.

Review the selects against the sentence, not against whether you like the color. If the sentence survives, keep the frame. If you are keeping it because the light is nice, you are decorating. Decoration can sit in the margins. It should not take the hero.

## Crop, interface, and honesty

Crop to the decision. The button, the status, the amount, the owner. Extra chrome that does not serve the job can go, as long as you do not invent a layout the product does not have. Removing a sidebar in a crop is different from drawing a new product.

Leave enough type that a reader believes the tool is real. A crop so tight that it becomes abstract shapes is a texture, not a product. Pull back until a stranger can tell what kind of record they are seeing.

Color and type in the photograph should match the product you ship. A graded, peach-tinted version of a cool interface is a second brand. Operators notice. They will wonder which one they would log into. Photograph the real theme. If the brand site is quiet and the product is dense, let that be visible. Density, when it is the point, is a claim. A trading interface, including a public concept such as Trade Moai, has a job that may need a dense frame. Do not thin the evidence into a lifestyle crop.

Alt text is part of honesty. The W3C WCAG overview treats text alternatives as a basic requirement so people who cannot see the image still get the content. Describe what is in the frame. "An approval queue with one invoice waiting on a finance manager." Do not paste the keyword into the alt. Do not say "image of innovation." The alt is a sentence for a person.

## When a stock frame is the wrong argument

Stock can fill a hole on a deadline. It rarely carries a product claim, because the product was not in the room when the photo was taken. If you use a stock frame at all, use it where the claim is about a place or a material, and even then, prefer a picture you directed.

For the hero, wait. A short page with one real screen is stronger than a finished-looking page with a rented team. Publish the screen. Add the human frame when you have a real session to shoot. The absence will look intentional if the screen is good. The stock will look like a cover.

Keep a small library once you have real frames. The hero screen. One admin. One detail of the record. Reuse them so the site feels like one place. A new stock photo per section feels like a collage of other companies. Consistency is a form of proof.

## Place the pictures where the argument needs them

The first screen gets the product in use. Later sections get the pictures that answer the next question. A second screen for a second step. A person only when you are naming who does the work. A detail crop when a field is the whole point.

Do not interrupt a pricing table with a mood photograph. The table is the argument there. A picture beside it should be the plan in the product, or nothing. Silence is a legitimate design choice. Not every section has earned a frame.

Give each picture a caption that states the claim, and end the credit in the way your process requires. The caption is for the operator. It can be one sentence. "The manager approves from the queue. The side path we refused is not on this screen."

The photographs have to survive the width where the visit actually happens. A wide hero that becomes a postage stamp on a phone has lost the claim. Read [how the mobile visit should still show the product and the demo](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you approve a crop that only works on a laptop.
